Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Policy Analyst
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Adebayo sits perfectly still in his chair, a man whose professional life as a policy analyst has been defined by composure and careful thought. At sixty-eight, he still carries the erect posture of someone accustomed to boardrooms and briefing documents, but a subtle tension in his shoulders and the way his gaze never fully settles betray a profound internal disquiet. Eight months ago, his body, the one vessel he had always taken for granted, tried to kill him. He had been at home, alone in the quiet house that felt cavernous since his wife passed, reading a report on municipal water rights. The first sensation was not pain, but a dense, crushing pressure in his chest, as if a great weight had been placed upon him. His breath shortened, and a cold sweat bloomed on his forehead. In the disorienting chaos of the ambulance ride and the fluorescent glare of the emergency room, the world narrowed to the frantic beeping of monitors and the terrifying feeling of his own heart failing. He survived, but the man who left the hospital was not the same one who had been rushed there.

In the weeks that followed, the initial relief of survival was slowly eroded by a creeping, pervasive dread. Adebayo returned to his work at the think tank, but found he could no longer follow the intricate threads of legislative analysis. He would sit at his desk, staring at a page of dense text, and his mind would simply refuse to engage. The words would blur, his focus snagged by the rhythm of his own pulse or a fleeting flutter in his chest. His body felt like a separate, hostile entity, humming with a constant, low-level alarm. Even in the safety of his own home, he felt perpetually on guard, every muscle braced for the next betrayal. He started checking his pulse obsessively, interpreting any skipped beat or moment of light-headedness as a prelude to another attack. He had come to believe that his body was fundamentally unreliable, a traitor that could turn on him without warning.

The memories of that night are not consistent. When his cardiologist asks for the details, Adebayo can recount the sequence of events with a strange, sterile detachment. He lists the symptoms, the 911 call, the intubation, feeling completely numb as he speaks, as if narrating a case study about a stranger. But at other times, the memory ambushes him. A scene in a movie with hospital lights, the sound of a distant siren, or even just a moment of indigestion can trigger it. Suddenly, he is no longer in his living room but back in the ER, the crushing pressure blooming in his chest, the metallic taste of fear in his mouth. It feels utterly real, happening right now, and the wave of terror is so absolute that he has to stand up and pace the room, gasping for air, just to convince himself it is over.

This constant state of alert has scoured out most other feelings. He looks at photographs of his late wife, a woman he adored for forty years, and feels a hollow ache where love and grief used to be. It is this emotional emptiness that frightens him most. He is certain that the trauma has permanently broken his capacity for normal emotion, leaving him with only two settings: high-alert terror or a vacant numbness. This belief has reshaped his life. He stopped taking his customary evening walks, terrified that the exertion would trigger another cardiac event. At work, he takes the elevator to his second-floor office, avoiding the stairs. His adult children call, their voices thick with concern, but he keeps the conversations short, their questions about his health feeling like probes into a wound. The isolation he felt after his wife’s death has now become a fortress. A recent performance review at work, citing his lack of focus and missed deadlines, was the final impetus for seeking help. Adebayo now sits in a therapist’s office, a man trapped in a ceasefire with his own body, terrified that he will never again feel safe inside his own skin.
